newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE euroyen ends higher as rate fears disappear.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE euroyen ends higher as rate fears disappear.

text.p: June 11 settlement prev settlement
TIFFE Euroyen 3M (Z) 99.05 98.96

Key December three-month euroyen interest rate futures surged by Wednesday's close as the yen's sharp rise wiped away an earlier view that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) may raise interest rates in the coming months.

"The December's rise above 99.00 represents a growing view in the market that the BOJ would not raise its discount rate by the year-end, although it may stop guiding the key short-term interest rate by then," said a long-term credit bank dealer.
"If the dollar falls below 110 yen, the key Nikkei stock average may plunge below the 20,000 yen level. Then the December may challenge 99.10," the dealer said.
The stronger yen eased fears of higher interest rates as it would hinder a recovery in Japan's economy, traders said.
The December settled up 0.09 at a session high of 99.05 on Wednesday, which was the highest settlement since April 22.
Turnover was a hefty 142,463 contracts.
The recent fall in the December started when the Nikkei rose above 20,000 in early May. On Wednesday, the Nikkei index ended down 242.62 point or 1.18 percent at 20,189.93.
The contract has been in an uptrend since late May due to a series of announcements of weak Japanese economic data.

The yen's sharp rise also encouraged Japanese banks to change their positions in the interest rate swap (IRS) market, traders said. The dollar fell as low as 110.81 yen, its lowest level since November 18, 1996, this afternoon after a sharp rise in Japan's sensitive current account surplus fuelled worries over trade tension.
Two- and three-year IRS rates fell sharply as Japanese banks that had been paying fixed interest rates earlier were mostly on the receiving side, traders said.
Three-year IRS rates were quoted at 1.49/1.53 percent as of 0738 GMT against Tuesday's 1.61/1.65 percent. Two-year IRS rates were at 1.17/1.21 percent, down from 1.29/1.33 percent.
Traders said the BOJ's operation was more accommodative on Wednesday than in previous days in the face of the recent rise in interest rates with maturities of two weeks or longer.
Strong demand from banks to roll-over maturing long-term funds they had borrowed before March 31, 1997, provided the recent firmness in the overall money market rates, they said.
A total of some 19 trillion yen worth of certificates of deposit (CDs) are expected to mature this month.

But less than 700 billion yen in CDs has been issued so far this month. On Wednesday, some 310 billion yen in two-month CDs was issued at 0.59 percent, while around 40 billion yen in the key three-month CDs was issued at 0.60 percent, traders said.
The issued rates were unchanged from previous levels. Without the BOJ's very accommodative operation this morning, CD rates could have risen further, traders said.
Buyers of the CDs were mostly bank dealers, they said.
Investors preferred one-month CDs over two- or three-month CDs, as the longer maturities have greater exposure to a possible change in BOJ monetary policy.
"The BOJ operation showed the bank's intention of easing the recent upward pressure on interest rates due to an increasing demand for funds," said a city bank dealer.

But some said Wednesday's operation was aimed at taming concern in the market over Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd, which was hit by a scandal involving suspected racketeer payoffs and has been aggressively securing long-term funds.

The BOJ left the market in surplus by some 300 billion yen, up from a surplus of 200 billion in previous days. The key overnight call rate was mainly traded at 0.47 percent, down from Tuesday's 0.49. -- Risa Maeda +81-3-3432-8570
